title: Nirvana Day again

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rohatsu: a week of sitting that ends when the morning star comes up. Your line was the morning star. Did you sit a little longer, or catch the sky before it got light? Today, the same life, at its other end. Day one thousand four hundred twenty-two.

A doctor comes home from a long trip and finds his children rolling on the floor. While he was away, they drank poison. Some of them still have their wits, and they take the medicine he mixes. The others, their minds turned, won't touch it. So the doctor does something strange. He leaves again, and sends a messenger home with news: your father is dead. You met this story in the Lotus Sutra this year. It comes back today, on Nirvana Day, the day the Buddha's passing is remembered, because the Lotus tells it about that very passing.
screen: `CHILDREN WHO DRANK POISON.` → `THEY REFUSE THE MEDICINE.` → `YOUR FATHER IS DEAD.`

segments.voice: The schools you met this year share one scene: the Buddha lying down between two sal trees at Kusinara, and his last instruction, which in paraphrase says that everything put together comes apart, so keep going with care. What the schools do with that scene is where this year comes in. Start with the Pali texts the Theravada keeps. A short book of sayings, the Itivuttaka, speaks of two elements of nibbana. One is nibbana with something remaining: an awakened person still alive, still feeling pleasant and painful things, but with greed, hatred and delusion gone. The other is nibbana with nothing remaining, when that life ends and all that was felt simply grows cool. In that reading, the passing is real and complete. A fire has gone out. Next, the Lotus Sutra. In its chapter on the lifespan of the Tathagata, the Buddha says he awoke immeasurable ages ago, and that his passing is a skillful means. If he stayed in plain sight, people would grow careless, sure he'd always be around. So, like the doctor, he appears to go. In their grief the children come to their senses and drink the medicine. Then, the story says, the father comes home. Third, the Diamond Sutra, near its end. It says the Tathagata doesn't come from anywhere and doesn't go anywhere, and that, it says, is why he is called the Tathagata. Three readings, side by side. A fire gone out. A doctor who seems to leave. A coming and going that was never quite either. Teachers in each school explain their own reading with care, and this path doesn't rank them. Some readers hear one thing they share with those last words: each ending is put to work, to wake the ones still here. Even the reading where the Buddha never really left needs the ending to look real, or nobody takes the medicine.
screen: `TWO ELEMENTS OF NIBBANA.` · `THE DOCTOR SEEMS TO LEAVE.` · `NEITHER COMING NOR GOING.` · then, large: `AN ENDING THAT WAKES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: reflect on endings. Sit, and let the breath find its own pace. Notice that each out-breath ends. Let three or four of them finish completely before the next one starts. Then let one ending from this past year come to mind. A job, a habit, a home, a friend who moved away, an older version of you. Ask it the doctor's question: did this ending wake anything up? Don't push for an answer. If nothing comes, that's fine. If sadness comes, let it sit beside you. Then come back to the breath, ending and beginning, until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Nirvana Day. The day remembering the Buddha's final passing, his parinirvana, kept on different calendars and read in different ways by the schools. Today's word.

Your line: all things end. Today, finish one small thing on purpose: end a call, close a book, set down a cup, and give that ending one full breath before the next thing. Day one thousand four hundred twenty-two.

howItsDone: In Japan and other East Asian communities, temples keep Nirvana Day with chanting, sutra reading and a painted scroll of the passing; in Theravada lands the passing is remembered on Vesak together with the birth and the awakening.

match.prompt: one passing, three readings: tap the pairs.
pairs: a doctor who seems to leave

myth: in the Lotus story, all the poisoned children take the medicine right away
some refuse it; only the news of their father's death brings them to their senses.
the Itivuttaka speaks of nibbana with something remaining and with nothing remaining
the first while an awakened person still lives; the second when that life ends.
this path names one school's reading of the passing as the right one
each school explains its own reading, and none is ranked.

fork.setup: you're the doctor. your children drank poison, and some refuse the medicine you made. what do you do?
options: leave, and send word that you have died.
wait at home until they change their minds.
fork.reveal: in the Lotus Sutra he goes away and sends word of his death. in their grief they take the medicine, and then he comes home.

original.note: Pali parinibbana (Sanskrit parinirvana): the final nirvana at an awakened one's death.

trapdoor: what you thought: Nirvana Day is a memorial day for the Buddha.
what it means: the passing remembered, and read three ways: a fire gone out, a doctor's skillful means, neither coming nor going.
what a scholar hears: Itivuttaka 44's two nibbana elements, the lifespan chapter of the Lotus (Kern ch. 15), and section 29 of the Diamond Sutra.

sources.ref: Mahaparinibbana Sutta, Digha Nikaya 16 (the sal trees at Kusinara; the last words)
Saddharma-pundarika, Kern ch. 15 (the lifespan of the Tathagata; the physician's sons)

notes: Index title has no word; word kept as 'Nirvana Day again'.
Itivuttaka 44 paraphrased: nibbana-element with residue remaining (sa-upadisesa) and without residue (anupadisesa), 'all that is felt ... will become cool'. Please confirm the paraphrase.

Lotus Sutra physician parable placed in Kern's ch. 15 (Duration of Life of the Tathagata), matching day 1170 of this path. Confirm chapter number in Kern and that the father returns after the sons recover.
Diamond Sutra section 29 (Müller 1894) paraphrased: the Tathagata neither comes nor goes, and is therefore called Tathagata. Confirm section number in Müller's division.
Practice keeps endings general; a Keeper may wish to check that the 'did this ending wake anything up?' question is not heard as minimizing grief.
Original: Pali parinibbana in Devanagari (परिनिब्बान); confirm spelling and stress.
Editor: softened 'every school' to 'the schools you met'; reworded the closing claim that each reading 'uses an ending to wake someone up' (the Itivuttaka does not say this) to 'some readers hear'.
